title: Education Dave Stuart Jr. A Collaborative Approach for Crafting Everest Statements With Your Students
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Dave Stuart Jr. shares a case study from Mandy, a Brooklyn English teacher who ran a 'School: Why Bother?' mini-unit at the start of the school year, culminating in collaboratively constructed Everest statements (class mission statements) for each period. The mini-unit, Stuart argues, activates three key motivational factors from his book The Will to Learn: Value (students explore why school matters), Efficacy (articulating a vision of success strengthens belief in reaching it), and Belonging (student voices become central from day one). Mandy's feedback reveals a striking result: the class that developed a strong collective mission became her favourite to teach -- 'willing to wrestle with big ideas, to be vulnerable, and to take risks' -- while the other class remained more guarded. The case study illustrates how beginning-of-year practices that treat school's value as a genuine question -- not a given -- create conditions for deeper engagement all year. Stuart closes by inviting teachers to try this approach and signals Mandy plans to expand it by having students co-create class AI policies.
points: * Collaboratively creating an Everest statement (class mission) at the start of the year simultaneously activates Value (students grapple with why school matters), Efficacy (defining success makes it more reachable), and Belonging (student voices shape the classroom identity from day one). * Beginning-of-year apologetics for school -- treating skepticism about school's purpose as a reasonable and respectable position -- create stronger long-term buy-in than assuming motivation; starting with 'School: why bother?' is more honest and more effective. * The difference between Mandy's two class periods demonstrates that early collaborative identity work has lasting effects on classroom culture: the class with stronger buy-in was more willing to take risks and engage deeply for the remainder of the year. * Everest statements are most powerful when they emerge from student language rather than teacher language; the process signals to students that their thinking and voices are constitutive parts of the class, not just inputs to be managed. * The mini-unit points toward a natural extension: having students co-create class AI policies alongside their mission statements, building shared norms around both purpose and tools from the very beginning of the year.
quotes: I'm really glad I started the year this project. It set the tone for the class in surprising ways. I teach two sections of 10th grade English, and their different outcomes and levels of buy-in really became clear when we co-created our class mission statements, five days into the school year.
This has become the class I most look forward to teaching every day -- they are willing to wrestle with big ideas, to be vulnerable, and to take risks.
I have found that this class is more guarded and less willing to take chances. They want to get their work done, but they're less interested in engaging with it.

I'm definitely going to keep incorporating this mini-unit into my beginning-of-year curriculum, and next year I think I will expand and combine it with a project I have done for the past two years and have students also co-create a class AI policy at the same time.
Good apologetics start with a simple foundation: skepticism is a reasonable and respectable point of view.
Most of our students who struggle with Efficacy do so because success is a vague and unexplored idea.
All this work quickly signals to students that their thinking and words and voices are important parts of the class they enter each day, which cultivates Belonging.
